Inspecting hardware across customer programs
Fraen Corporation designs and manufactures precision optics, lighting, and mechanical
assemblies that ship into automotive and aerospace programs. As a Quality Engineering
Co-op, I sat at the point where incoming and in-process parts got checked against print
before they moved further down the line, work which touched components bound for
several of Fraen's customer programs.

callouts to confirm parts met print before sign-off.

B E Y O N D T H E M E A S U R E M E N T
What I brought to the engineering team
Root Cause & Corrective Action
When inspection data flagged a defect or a drift in a process, I ran root cause
analysis on the variation and worked directly with manufacturing and
engineering to design and verify corrective actions —closing the loop
between what the measurement system caught and what actually changed
on the line.
Cross-Team Translation
Quality sits in the middle of a plant: I regularly translated the same finding
into whatever language a given team needed —a corrective-action ticket for
manufacturing, a drawing-callout question for design engineering, a trend for
the program's quality lead.
Documentation Discipline
Documented findings to a standard that would hold up under a customer
audit —precise, traceable, and consistent across every customer program I
touched.
Working Under Pressure
Prioritized across competing deadlines from multiple programs at once, and
stayed precise and even-keeled when a measurement disagreed with what
the floor expected to hear.

DANT E V AR ANO · E NGI NE ERING P ORTFOL IO
A N I N T E R A C T I V E B I O L U M I N E S C E N C E E X H I B I T
Gamifying a real survival mechanism
Built for Northeastern's Cornerstone of Engineering exhibit, Predator Escape gamifies
how deep-sea animals like lanternfish and the Atolla jellyfish use a burst of
bioluminescent light to startle a predator in the split second before it strikes. A console
runs a randomized five-LED “predator approaching” sequence; up to four players, each
on their own arcade-button controller have to react inside a difficulty-scaled window,
500 ms down to 195 ms, or the predator gets them.
My scope: the CAD for the console and controller enclosures, the full Arduino game
logic, and the MATLAB app that visualizes and logs it.

H A R D W A R E D E S I G N
CAD for the console & controllers
Every enclosure started as a SolidWorks model before it touched a laser cutter or a 3D printer. Concept selection ran through a Kepner-Tregoe Decision
Analysis (KTDA) matrix, weighing candidate exhibit mechanics against reliability, safety, cost, and ease of fabrication.
Circuit & Console Housing
Footprint: 9.00 × 6.10 in
Screen cutout: 4.00 × 2.00 in
LED bores: Ø.20 in, 5×
Controller & Button Housing
Footprint: 3.00 × 4.00 in
Depth: 2.50 in
Button bore: Ø1.20 in
DANT E V AR ANO · E NGI NE ERING P ORTFOL IO 08
S O F T W A R E —E M B E D D E D & V I S U A L I Z A T I O N
Arduino firmware + MATLAB interface
The Arduino firmware runs the entire game loop on an Uno: it opens a join
window, runs the randomized predator sequence, times every player's
reaction against a difficulty-scaled window, and eliminates whoever missed
it. It emits plain-text tokens over serial —START_SEQUENCE, STEP:n,
END_SEQUENCE —that a MATLAB App Designer interface listens for to stay
in sync, swapping the on-screen predator image to match the physical LED
countdown and logging every reaction time to a timestamped CSV.
INPUT_PULLUP debounced buttons
Serial handshake protocol
Difficulty-scaled reaction windows
Live top-5 leaderboard + CSV logging
reactionGameVisualizer() —predator image synced to the LED sequence
My individual contribution, from the Cornerstone II technical report:
“My main contributions were focused on drafting game code, laser cutting, and MATLAB integration — smoothing out the game's functionality, adding features that
allowed 1–4 players to play, level selection, and a GUI display.”

100% Button-press & LED sequence reliability
Final exhibition (April 11, 2025): 37 total gameplay sessions, 142 individual rounds, average reaction time 278 ms across all players. Assembled system (console + four controllers): ~24 × 24 in
footprint, under 5 lbs.
Honest gap: players came away able to describe an animal that uses bioluminescence, but fewer connected that back to the predator-escape mechanic itself —next iteration
folds a one-line “why this matters” prompt into the win/lose screen.

R E T R O S P E C T I V E
If I built it again
SYNC FIX
Cue LEDs from MATLAB
Shift the predator-image / LED handoff so MATLAB
drives the cue instead of Arduino, removing the serial-
processing delay that occasionally broke sync.
AESTHETICS
Brighter, bigger presentation
A larger trifold and a brighter enclosure color scheme,
with controller colors matched to their LED/button
pairing.
SENSORY CUES
Add sound
The exhibit only covered sight and touch, so voice
prompts or suspense music would engage a third sense.
Personally, I logged roughly 70–80 hours on this project across the semester and put in a personal laptop (over $1,000 in value) plus $5.29 for laser-cut
wood, keeping the team under its $100 cost / $1,000 value budget cap. The part I was proudest of was getting the serial link between the Arduino and
MATLAB working cleanly, which was the piece that turned four independent buttons and some LEDs into an actual synced, data-logging exhibit.

Y A W K E Y B O Y S & G I R L S C L U B
Mentoring, logistics, and outreach
Roxbury Robotics brings hands-on robotics programming to Boston middle
schoolers at the Yawkey Boys & Girls Club. I serve on the executive board as
secretary and lead mentor: running weekly workshops, managing site logistics,
organizing volunteers, and keeping meeting notes, communications, and
scheduling on track.
Running the Showcase
Helped organize and run a robotics showcase at the Yawkey Boys & Girls Club for all of the
students in the program, coordinating logistics, setting up competition stations, and keeping
the day moving.
Club Outreach
Helped with outreach for the club by representing Roxbury Robotics to bring in new students,
volunteers, and support so the program can keep reaching more kids.

S H O W C A S E C H A L L E N G E
Rainforest Rescue —200 points, 4 tasks
Students programmed their robots to run a rainforest-conservation themed course
worth 200 points across four tasks:
Avoiding Vulnerable Habitat 10 + 25 pts
Put Out the Fire 65 + 20 pts
Shining the Flashlight 10 + 10 pts
Replant Deforested Area (3 saplings) 20 pts × 3 = 60 pts
TOTAL AVAILABLE 200 pts
